title: Management of Payables (Creditors)
outcomes: Explain trade credit and its costs and benefits.
Compute the cost of forgoing cash discounts.
Apply good payables practices including MSME rules.

meta.exam_tip: Always compare the cost of forgoing a discount with the borrowing rate given.

concepts.title: Trade credit as a source of finance
body: Trade credit is a spontaneous short-term source of finance arising from normal purchases; it grows automatically with business volume and needs no formal agreement.
Costs of using it: discounts forgone, loss of goodwill if terms are overstepped, administrative costs and conditions such as minimum order sizes.
Costs of not using it: interest cost of paying early (trade credit is otherwise interest-free), and with inflation, paying later in money of lower value is beneficial.
concepts.analogy: Supplier credit is cheap money — until you give up a discount for it.
concepts.work: A retailer taking 30 days' credit on ₹10 lakh of monthly purchases effectively borrows ₹10 lakh interest-free.

concepts.title: Cost of forgoing cash discounts
body: Simple annual cost of forgoing a discount = [d ÷ (100 − d)] × (365 ÷ t), where d is the discount % and t the extra days of credit obtained (credit period − discount period).
Effective annual cost, allowing for compounding = (100 ÷ (100 − d))^(365 ÷ t) − 1.
Decision: if the cost of forgoing exceeds the firm's cost of borrowing (or return on alternative investment), take the discount; otherwise use the full credit period.
concepts.analogy: A small discount for a short wait can carry a very high annual cost.
concepts.work: "1/10, net 30" costs about 18.4% a year if forgone.

concepts.title: Managing payables in practice
body: Good practice: pay on the due date (not earlier, not later), negotiate better terms with key suppliers, centralise payments, and use electronic payments.
Monitor creditors' days and ageing; avoid stretching payables, which damages reputation and supply.

Small suppliers (MSMEs) must be paid within the agreed period subject to a maximum of 45 days under the MSMED Act, with interest at three times the bank rate on delays, and companies report MSME dues; delayed MSME payments also affect tax deductibility of the expense.
concepts.analogy: Payables management is about timing and trust, not just delay.
concepts.work: A firm that delays MSME payments beyond 45 days faces penal interest and disclosure.

solution.title: Cost of trade credit

solution.text: Forgoing the discount costs about 25–28% a year, far above the 14% bank rate. Borrow from the bank and pay on day 15.

illustrations.title: How long do we take to pay?
illustrations.q: Average trade creditors ₹6 lakh; annual credit purchases ₹48.67 lakh. Compute creditors' days (365-day year) and comment if supplier terms are 45 days.

solution.text: The firm pays in about 45 days — in line with terms. Stretching further could strain supplier relations and lose discounts.

jobs.title: Discount policy
jobs.situation: Procurement wants to know which supplier discounts to take.
steps: Compute the annual cost of forgoing each.
Compare with the bank borrowing rate.
jobs.takeaway: Take any discount whose forgone cost exceeds the cost of borrowing.

mcqs.q: Trade credit is called a spontaneous source because it:
mcqs.explain: It rises and falls with purchases without negotiation each time. In practice: grows with sales.
mcqs.topic: Trade credit as a source of finance

mcqs.q: Simple annual cost of forgoing "2/10, net 30" (365 days):
mcqs.explain: 2/98 × 365/20 = 37.24%. In practice: almost always worth taking.
t is the extra days gained by not taking the discount. In practice: 30 − 10 = 20 for "2/10, net 30".

mcqs.q: If the cost of forgoing a discount is 20% and bank interest is 12%, the firm should:
options: Take the discount using bank funds
mcqs.explain: Borrowing at 12% to save 20% is profitable. In practice: check bank limits.

mcqs.q: Stretching payables beyond terms may cause:
options: Loss of supplier goodwill and discounts
mcqs.explain: Suppliers may restrict supply or credit. In practice: reputation matters.

mcqs.q: Under the MSMED Act the maximum agreed payment period to MSME suppliers is:
mcqs.explain: Payment must be within the agreed period, not beyond 45 days. In practice: interest at three times bank rate applies on delay.

mcqs.q: Average creditors ₹4 lakh; credit purchases ₹36.5 lakh (365 days). Creditors' days:
mcqs.explain: 4 ÷ (36.5 ÷ 365) = 4 ÷ 0.1 = 40 days. In practice: compare with supplier terms.

mcqs.q: The compound cost of forgoing a discount is:
mcqs.explain: Compounding over multiple periods in a year raises the effective cost. In practice: use for precise comparisons.

Take discount if its cost exceeds borrowing cost.
Pay on due date; MSME limit 45 days.
traps: Using the full credit period as t.

viva.q: Why is trade credit not free?
viva.model: Because using the full credit period often means forgoing a cash discount, and overstepping terms damages goodwill.
Discount divided by one hundred minus discount, multiplied by 365 divided by the extra days of credit.

viva.q: When should a discount be taken?
viva.model: When the annual cost of forgoing it is higher than the firm's cost of borrowing or its return on surplus funds.

viva.q: What is the MSMED Act requirement on payments?
viva.model: Payments to micro and small suppliers must be made within the agreed period, not exceeding 45 days, with penal interest on delays.

viva.q: Name one good practice in managing payables.
viva.model: Paying on the due date rather than early or late, while negotiating better terms with key suppliers.

cases.title: Metro Electricals
cases.case: Metro Electricals buys ₹1.2 crore a year from a supplier offering "1/10, net 40". Its overdraft rate is 11%. It currently pays on day 40.

mcqs.q: Simple annual cost of forgoing the discount:
mcqs.explain: 1/99 × 365/30 = 12.29%. In practice: slightly above overdraft cost.

options: Yes, as 12.29% exceeds the 11% overdraft rate
Only if it has surplus cash
mcqs.explain: Borrowing at 11% to avoid a 12.29% cost is beneficial. In practice: margin is thin, so check limits.
1% of ₹1.2 crore = ₹1,20,000. In practice: offset extra interest on 30 days' funds.

mcqs.q: Extra interest from paying 30 days earlier (₹, approx.):
mcqs.explain: Average extra borrowing ≈ 1.19 crore × 30/365 ≈ ₹9.8 lakh × 11% ≈ ₹1.07 lakh — less than ₹1.2 lakh saved. In practice: net gain about ₹13,000.
